overview: Both are electron microscopes, but they image specimens differently — one sees through the sample, the other scans its surface.
genZNote: TEM: X-ray vision, sees the inside. SEM: takes a detailed 3D photo of the surface.

aspects.label: Imaging Method
aspects.valueA: Electrons pass through an ultra-thin specimen, forming a 2D image of internal structure.
aspects.valueB: Electrons scan across the specimen's surface, and reflected/emitted electrons build a 3D-like surface image.

aspects.label: Sample Requirement
aspects.valueA: Requires extremely thin sections (as thin as 100 nm).
aspects.valueB: Can image whole, thicker specimens since only the surface is imaged.

aspects.label: Type of Image Produced
aspects.valueA: Detailed 2D cross-sectional image, showing internal ultrastructure.
aspects.valueB: Detailed 3D-like topographic image of the surface.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: TEM is used to study internal cell organelle structure; SEM is used to study surface texture, such as pollen grains or a virus's surface coat.
overlay.memoryTrick: TEM = Transmission = electrons go THROUGH, internal view. SEM = Scanning = electrons scan the SURFACE.
overlay.commonMisconception: SEM does not typically achieve the same ultra-fine resolution as TEM for internal structures — it excels at surface topography, not internal detail.
